# Any Repeat in the Array? — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/arrays-hashing/contains-duplicate.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Arrays & Hashing** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate/)

Given an integer array, return true if any value appears at least twice, and false if every element is distinct.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
- -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
- a single element cannot repeat, so a one-element array is always false
- values are unbounded in range but bounded in count — there is no room to index by value

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]` | `true` | 1 appears twice. |
| `nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]` | `false` | All distinct. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. You do not need to know WHICH value repeats, or how often — only whether one does.
2. Walk once and remember what you have already seen. What structure answers 'have I seen this?' in constant time?
3. The moment a value is already in the set, you can return — there is nothing left to learn.

</details>

---

## 1. Brute force

Compare every pair of positions and return true the first time two of them hold the same value.

```python
def contains_duplicate(nums: list[int]) -> bool:
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] == nums[j]:
                return True
    return False
```

**O(n²) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean containsDuplicate(int[] nums) {
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) {
            if (nums[i] == nums[j]) return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool containsDuplicate(const vector<int>& nums) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
            if (nums[i] == nums[j]) return true;
        }
    }
    return false;
}
```

</details>

---

## 2. Sort first

> **Why now.** The nested scan re-reads the whole tail for every element. Sorting collapses the question to a single comparison per position — but it pays O(n log n) and destroys the original order to do it.

Sort the array, then walk it once: duplicates, if there are any, must end up side by side.

```python
def contains_duplicate(nums: list[int]) -> bool:
    ordered = sorted(nums)
    for i in range(1, len(ordered)):
        if ordered[i] == ordered[i - 1]:
            return True
    return False
```

**O(n log n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean containsDuplicate(int[] nums) {
    int[] ordered = nums.clone();
    Arrays.sort(ordered);
    for (int i = 1; i < ordered.length; i++) {
        if (ordered[i] == ordered[i - 1]) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool containsDuplicate(const vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<int> ordered = nums;
    sort(ordered.begin(), ordered.end());
    for (size_t i = 1; i < ordered.size(); i++) {
        if (ordered[i] == ordered[i - 1]) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
```

</details>

---

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Sorting pays O(n log n) to put duplicates next to each other, but adjacency was never the question. A set answers 'seen before?' directly, and the early return means a duplicate near the front costs almost nothing.

Walk the array once carrying a set of the values seen so far. Before adding a value, ask whether it is already there; if it is, the answer is true and the rest of the array is irrelevant. If the walk finishes, every value was distinct. The set costs O(n) memory, which is the price of not having to sort.

```python
def contains_duplicate(nums: list[int]) -> bool:
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public boolean containsDuplicate(int[] nums) {
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (!seen.add(x)) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
bool containsDuplicate(const vector<int>& nums) {
    unordered_set<int> seen;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (seen.count(x)) return true;
        seen.insert(x);
    }
    return false;
}
```

</details>

---

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brute force | O(n²) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Sort first | O(n log n) time · O(1) space | The nested scan re-reads the whole tail for every element. Sorting collapses the question to a single comparison per position — but it pays O(n log n) and destroys the original order to do it. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(n) space | Sorting pays O(n log n) to put duplicates next to each other, but adjacency was never the question. A set answers 'seen before?' directly, and the early return means a duplicate near the front costs almost nothing. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def contains_duplicate_brute_force(nums: list[int]) -> bool:
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] == nums[j]:
                return True
    return False


def contains_duplicate_sort_first(nums: list[int]) -> bool:
    ordered = sorted(nums)
    for i in range(1, len(ordered)):
        if ordered[i] == ordered[i - 1]:
            return True
    return False


def contains_duplicate_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int]) -> bool:
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

APPROACHES = [
    contains_duplicate_brute_force,
    contains_duplicate_sort_first,
    contains_duplicate_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# the early return on a repeat — [1,1] repeats at the second element, [1,2,3,4] never does
CASES = [
    lambda: ([1,2,3,1],),
    lambda: ([1,2,3,4],),
    lambda: ([1],),
    lambda: ([1,1],),
    lambda: ([-1,0,-1,5],),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<40} -> {answers}")
```
